companions.why: A zener regulates by conducting; with nothing limiting the current it dissipates until it fails.

rules.why: A two-terminal part with one leg on no net is not in the circuit.
A diode installed backwards blocks the current the circuit needs and conducts the one it does not.

companions.why: Each supply pin needs a local ceramic to supply the switching current the rail cannot deliver fast enough; without it the die sees its own supply collapse on every edge.
One bulk capacitor per device holds the rail up through load steps the decoupling caps are too small for.

rules.why: A supply or return pin that reaches no net means the part is unpowered.
Two drivers on one net fight; whichever is stronger sources the other's short-circuit current.
An output tied straight to a supply or ground is a short the moment it drives the other way.
Pins the symbol groups into one domain landing on different nets is usually a wiring slip, occasionally deliberate.

The radio draws hundreds of milliamps in bursts. A rail without real bulk capacitance browns out on the first transmit and the part resets.
EN must be high for the part to run at all, and it has no internal pull-up.
The RC on EN delays release until the supply is up, which is what makes cold starts reliable.

The coil is an inductor. When the drive turns off, its collapsing field produces whatever voltage it takes to keep the current flowing — enough to destroy the transistor driving it.
The input side is an LED. Driven from a logic pin with no series resistor it takes the pin's whole current capability.
The output is a phototransistor: it can only pull down, so the receiving side needs a pull-up.
